analysis.one_liner: Makes drug makers repay Medicare for the unused portions of single-dose vials they bill for.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a hearing or a vote: it drew zero cosponsors and sat in two House committees until the Congress ended in January 2021.
analysis.plain_summary: When a doctor gives a Medicare patient a drug from a single-dose vial and some of the drug is thrown away, Medicare currently pays for the discarded amount — and the patient pays 20% coinsurance on it. This bill would make drug manufacturers rebate that wasted amount back to Medicare, and would stop billing patients coinsurance for drug that was never given to them. It never advanced past its committee referrals.
analysis.who_benefits: Medicare beneficiaries who receive doctor-administered drugs, especially expensive cancer drugs sold in single-dose vials, would pay coinsurance only on the portion actually administered instead of on the amount thrown away. The Medicare trust fund would gain because manufacturers' rebates would be deposited there, which lowers costs for all beneficiaries and taxpayers since premiums and general revenue finance the program.

how_it_helps.text: Manufacturers of single-source drugs and biologics sold in single-dose vials would have to pay Medicare a rebate each quarter for the discarded amounts — calculated as 90% of the wasted amount times the drug's average sales price or wholesale acquisition cost — with the money deposited into the Medicare trust fund.

Medicare would collect a patient's 20% coinsurance only on the portion of the drug actually administered, so beneficiaries would no longer pay out of pocket for drug that was discarded before it reached them.
The requirement is enforced: manufacturers face periodic audits and a civil money penalty equal to the unpaid rebate plus 25% if they fail to comply.
Doctors, hospitals, and clinics that administer the drugs would keep their full Medicare payment, including for discarded amounts, so providers would not lose income under the bill.

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name drug manufacturers that sell single-dose vial drugs paid for under Medicare Part B, who would lose the revenue they currently collect on the portion of each vial that gets thrown away.
analysis.who_pays_short: Brand-name makers of single-dose vial drugs

drawbacks.text: The rebate covers only 90% of the discarded amount, so manufacturers would still keep a slice of the revenue on drug that was wasted.

Providers would continue to be paid for discarded amounts, so the bill gives doctors and clinics no financial reason to choose vial sizes or dosing schedules that minimize waste — it targets only the manufacturer side.

Rebates are calculated from the manufacturer's own reported average sales price or wholesale acquisition cost, and drugs covered by 340B pricing agreements are carved out at a different price, which leaves room for pricing gamesmanship and complicates enforcement.
Manufacturers could respond to losing waste revenue by raising list prices, which would shift part of the cost back onto Medicare and patients over time.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is real but modest: it eliminates a patient-billing unfairness (paying coinsurance on drug they never received) and claws back public money spent on waste, at a direct cost only to the drug makers collecting that money. The design is imperfect — 10% of waste revenue stays with manufacturers and providers keep being paid for waste — but the drawbacks are smaller than the gains, and the bill died without any of them ever being weighed in a hearing or vote.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to two House committees and a health subcommittee in August 2019, no hearing or vote ever happened, and the bill died when the Congress ended in January 2021.

narrative.text: Rep. Eliot Engel introduced the bill on August 9, 2019, with no cosponsors.
The same day it was sent to the Energy and Commerce Committee and the Ways and Means Committee, and within days was referred to the Health Subcommittee.
No hearing, markup, or floor vote ever occurred; the last recorded action is the August 12, 2019 subcommittee referral, and the bill expired when the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name drug makers are better off: they continue to collect full Medicare payment, and patients continue to pay coinsurance, on drug discarded from single-dose vials.

sides.party_line_note: No vote ever occurred, and the bill attracted zero cosponsors from either party even though Democrats controlled the House.

industries.industry: Brand-name drug makers (single-source drugs and biologics in single-dose vials)
industries.note: These manufacturers currently get paid by Medicare for the full contents of each vial, including what is discarded, and patients pay coinsurance on the waste. The bill would force them to rebate roughly the full price of discarded amounts, backed by audits and a penalty of the unpaid rebate plus 25%. Their interest runs directly against patients' here: their revenue comes from billing for drug patients never received.

industries.industry: Providers that administer infused drugs (hospitals, oncology practices, infusion clinics)
industries.note: The bill explicitly leaves provider payments untouched, so they would keep full Medicare payment including for discarded amounts, but they would face new claim-modifier reporting and their patients would pay less in coinsurance.
